## Overview

- Portal hypertension is a major complication of many pediatric liver and vascular diseases
- Normal portal venous pressure: **5 to 10 mm Hg**
- Portal hypertension: portal venous pressure **exceeding 10 mm Hg**
- The **hepatic venous pressure gradient (HVPG)** is the accepted surrogate marker
- Management spans pharmacologic, endoscopic, and surgical options
- A multidisciplinary approach is often essential

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this presentation you will be able to:

1. Define portal hypertension and interpret HVPG values
2. Describe the pathophysiology of elevated portal pressure
3. Classify pediatric causes as prehepatic, hepatic, or posthepatic
4. Recognize the clinical presentations, including variceal bleeding, ascites, and hepatopulmonary syndrome
5. Outline prophylaxis and acute management of variceal hemorrhage
6. Understand the role of TIPS and the meso-Rex bypass

## Definition of Portal Hypertension

- Normal pressure in the portal venous system: **5–10 mm Hg**
- Portal hypertension is defined as portal venous pressure **greater than 10 mm Hg**
- Direct measurement of portal pressure is impractical, so **HVPG** is used as a surrogate marker
- Elevated portal pressure drives the formation of collaterals (varices), splenomegaly, and ascites

::: callout-important
Portal hypertension is not a diagnosis by itself — it is a hemodynamic state with many possible prehepatic, hepatic, and posthepatic causes.
:::

## Hepatic Venous Pressure Gradient (HVPG)

- HVPG is a **surrogate marker of portal hypertension**
- Normal HVPG: **1 to 4 mm Hg**
- Portal hypertension develops when HVPG is **more than 5 mm Hg**
- In adults, HVPG **greater than 10 mm Hg** predicts the development of varices

::: callout-note
Data are limited in children, but they suggest **similar pressure thresholds** for the development of complications in the pediatric population.
:::

## HVPG Thresholds at a Glance

| HVPG Value | Interpretation |
|---|---|
| 1–4 mm Hg | Normal |
| More than 5 mm Hg | Portal hypertension develops |
| More than 10 mm Hg | Predicts development of varices (adult data) |
| 12 mm Hg | Predicts risk of bleeding from esophageal varices (adult data) |

::: callout-warning
Most threshold data come from adults. Pediatric data are limited but point to comparable cutoffs.
:::

## The Portal System: Anatomy and Physiology

- The portal system is a **low-pressure venous system** carrying partially oxygenated blood to the liver
- The liver receives highly oxygenated blood through the **hepatic arteries**
- Both systems combine within the **sinusoidal spaces**
- This dual supply makes the sinusoid the key site where resistance can rise
